source_text: Yes, that's the one.  I did speak with him briefly after one of the talks, that's how I found out about his repos.  But, broadly this makes me think we could do a kind of Consumer Reports approach to these things: can we get them, can we build them, can we use them?  The cotal example is maybe: we could use that, but we could also diagram-chase a different solution, e.g., agents coordinating via Agency or Matrix, and that's fine.  The ipfs_accelerate might be: we do something a little similar in the work on the War Machine but this is cool and we should do it more often.  But that review would be pending a serious investigation.  Many of the others, if they are not open source, would be answered: "No we can't install them because they ask for money and I'm not prepared to spend anything on a service whose spec I don't trust".  But again, that's TBD.  Let's start by committing and completing the rest of the investigation, as you said.  In fact, this reminds me that one of the tools had an interesting list of verbs involved.  Maybe we could extend the xiaoxiang-insert-mark list of verbs with some more verbs that help understand what these tools actually do, so that we could build a network of intents.  In terms of a "thesis" broadly I'm not asserting that we're different from anything, just that we should be enabled and empowered by the best-of among open source ideas and solutions.

reply_text:
Mission committed (`189cb03`). I'm starting three research agents in parallel to write the Consumer Reports entries, one batch of about 18 entries each.Starting with Judgment Labs.Meanwhile I'm reading the 象 mark list to see how new verbs would fit into it.Starting with HydraDB.㊢ (committed) The HEAD is committed and pushed in futon0 as `189cb03`. It now includes your Consumer Reports format: can we get it, can we build it, can we use it, then a verdict. It also has your thesis and the cotal and ipfs_accelerate example verdicts in your words. I rewrote T1 to match: we're not claiming to be different, so the selection question is "who has an open idea FUTON would be better for having?"

㊢ ("complete the rest of the investigation") Three research agents are running in the background on about 54 entries, split into three batches:
- harnesses and coordination
- evals, verification and protocols
- memory, models and kindred projects

Each writes to `futon0/holes/missions/landscape/batch-{A,B,C}.md` as it goes. Every entry gets:
- a plain problem statement
- get / build / use, with licences checked against the actual repos
- the verbs the tool uses for what it does
- search seeds for finding other projects that solve the same problem

Batch C will also check the o-machine claim and confirm the JevOps ↔ TypeSafe link. I've left one item out: the serious ipfs_accelerate investigation. It needs reading the code, not the website, so I'd do it as a separate step.

㊟ ("extend the xiaoxiang-insert-mark list of verbs") I looked at `xiaoxiang-mark-keys`. There are 23 marks, and each is a *speech act* placed on a PBASE stage: report, propose, delegate, verify. The tools' verbs will mostly be *operations on work*: spawn, hand off, lease, admit, merge, replay. Only a few words appear on both lists, delegate and verify among them. Those shared verbs are where speech and work connect, so they'd be the links in the network of intents. I've written this up as T7. My suggestion is a separate operation vocabulary, linked to the marks only through the verbs the two lists share, so the `C-c ;` menu stays as it is. We can decide that once the verbs are collected.

🈯 ("an interesting list of verbs") Do you remember which tool had that verb list? If not, the agents are copying out any explicit verb list they find, and I'll flag the richest ones when they report back.

previous_reply_acts.text: (gist) The Lean one is Benjamin Barber's stack, the speaker from 10-09. It turns out the "TypeSafe AI / Jev" link in your room log belongs to him too, so those two entries are one lead. I read his GitHub READMEs and added him to the mission. Nothing was run.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-13
previous_reply_acts.text: ("Lean-backed dispatches") The Agency-like part is the "agent supervisor" inside `endomorphosis/ipfs_accelerate_py` (AGPL-3.0). It takes an objective and runs this chain: code and proof-gap analysis → todos → leases and isolated worktrees → LLM proposals → deterministic validation → merge receipts. His own wording is that LLM output is "proposal material". Nothing is admitted until a checker or prover signs off.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-13
previous_reply_acts.text: (the Jev link) His `JevOps` repo describes itself as the "TypeSafe / Jev kernel, split from Lean Refactor Arena". In it, an autoencoder proposes Lean candidates, and only Lean/Lake can admit them. That's the "autoencoders to produce Lean" from his talk. The current application is source-locked US federal law, which is the "Lean and law" part. His `Mcp-Plus-Plus` is a spec for making multi-agent tool calls auditable: content-addressed contracts, an event DAG for replay, and deontic policy. That sits close to the evidence store and the audit offer.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-13
previous_reply_acts.text: (why he stands out from the rest) Most of the log is harnesses, competing with Agency on orchestration. Barber's stack lines up with the thesis from the July probe: agents propose, a formal checker decides, and a receipt records it. The domain is law where ours is maths, and the plumbing is IPFS/P2P where ours is a hub plus XTDB. In the mission I've filed him as a probable "talk to", not as something to copy.
